backups.replicateDescription: Sends the backup files to a backup pool of a remote cluster. The copy there is an ordinary backup that can be restored on that cluster. An incremental backup is sent with the earlier backups of its chain that the remote cluster does not have yet, starting from the full backup. Deleting this backup deletes the copy too.

pools.createDescription: Where volumes are kept: a directory on each node, an NFS export that the nodes mount, an LVM thin pool or ZFS dataset on each node, a Ceph RBD pool, or a volume group shared by the nodes.
pools.pathHint: An absolute path on the nodes.

pools.makeSharedDescription: Only do this when every node of the pool sees the same files at {{path}}, such as an NFS share mounted outside Orbivisor. VMs with disks in the pool can then start on and migrate to any of its nodes.
pools.makeLocalDescription: Each volume goes back to the node that created it. VMs using the pool's volumes must be on that node and not migrating.

kindHint.dir: Create the directory on each node first.
kindHint.nfs: Each node mounts the export under its data directory. Mounting needs Linux nodes running as root. The pool is shared by its nodes.
kindHint.lvm-thin: Create the volume group and thin pool on each node first. Volumes are raw thin volumes kept on the node that creates them, and their snapshots hold disks only. Needs Linux nodes running as root.
kindHint.zfs: Create the dataset on each node first. Volumes are raw zvols kept on the node that creates them, and their snapshots hold disks only. Disks can only revert to their latest snapshot. Needs Linux nodes running as root.
kindHint.rbd: Create the Ceph pool first and put ceph.conf and the keyring on each node. Volumes are raw RBD images that every node of the pool can use, and their snapshots hold disks only. Needs Linux nodes with QEMU's rbd driver (qemu-block-extra) and the rbd command (ceph-common).
kindHint.lvm-shared: Create the shared volume group (vgcreate --shared) on a LUN every node sees first, and run lvmlockd with sanlock or dlm on each node. Volumes are raw logical volumes that every node of the pool can use, without snapshots. Needs Linux nodes running as root.

pools.optionsHint: Comma-separated options passed to mount -o after nosuid,nodev,noexec,retry=0, such as vers=4.2,hard.

kindHint.bridge: Plugs VMs straight into a bridge the node already has (such as vmbr0). Simplest; VMs only start on nodes with that bridge.
kindHint.vxlan: Joins all nodes with a tunnel so they share one network: a VM sees the same network on any node. Orbivisor creates the bridge on each node.
kindHint.sdn: A virtual switch spanning the nodes, with address ranges (subnets) and automatic addresses (DHCP). Attach it to a router to reach the outside.
kindHint.provider: An SDN network on the nodes' real physical network (untagged or a VLAN). Router outsides and floating IPs (external addresses) come from it. Administrators only.

networks.vniHint: The number that tells VXLAN networks apart (1–16777215). Pick one no other network uses.
networks.mtuHint: The largest packet sent at once. Empty means 1450 (1500 minus 50 bytes of tunnel header); usually leave it.
networks.vlanHint: A number that splits one switch into separate networks (1–4094). Empty means untagged. The switch port must be a trunk and the bridge must have VLAN awareness (vlan_filtering) on.
networks.userNote: The user network (QEMU NAT) is always available and is not listed.
networks.createDescription: Creates a network for VM network cards. If this is your first, 'bridge' is the simplest.
networks.deleteDescription: Bridges you created on the nodes are left alone. For a VXLAN network, Orbivisor removes its bridge and tunnel device from the nodes.

securityGroups.always: Always allowed: replies to allowed traffic, ARP, IPv6 neighbor discovery and DHCP replies. A VM can only send from its own MAC address.

fence.title: Force-isolate {{name}} when it fails (power off)
fence.description: When the node stops sending its heartbeat, the leader powers it off with these methods in order and starts its HA VMs on other nodes right away. If every method fails, it waits until the node stops itself (watchdog).
fence.none: No methods. When the node dies, the leader waits until it stops itself (watchdog, about 22 seconds by default — about 62 with the safe profile) before recovering.
fence.note: The leader powers nodes off, and neighbour nodes (regular checks), the testing node and the leader read the power, so every node must reach the BMC. IPMI needs ipmitool on every node. Commands get ORBIVISOR_NODE_NAME, ORBIVISOR_NODE_ID and ORBIVISOR_NODE_ADDRESS.

fence.systemIdHint: The server ID inside the management card. Leave empty when it has only one.
fence.insecure: Do not verify the BMC certificate
fence.offHint: Runs with /bin/sh -c on the leader to power the node off. A non-zero exit fails.
fence.statusHint: Prints off when the power is off and on when it is on, on its first line. Runs on neighbour nodes, the testing node and the leader.

vmForm.haRunning: Turn on HA while the VM is stopped.

haStateHint.started: If its node fails, HA starts the VM on another node.
haStateHint.stopped: If its node fails, HA moves the VM to another node but leaves it off.
haStateHint.ignored: HA leaves this VM alone for now: no isolation, recovery or counting. The settings are kept.

vmForm.haGroupHint: Recovers on the group's nodes, higher priority first.
vmForm.maxRestartHint: From 0 to 10 within 10 minutes. After that, HA moves the VM to another node.
vmForm.maxRelocateHint: From 0 to 10 within 10 minutes. After that, HA stops the VM and shows an error; start it again to clear it.
vmForm.haPriorityHint: From 0 to 100. When a node fails, HA restarts VMs with higher priority first.
vmForm.guestWatchHint: Asks the guest agent (qemu-guest-agent) whether the guest is alive and force-restarts the VM if it doesn't answer for the time below. Can be turned on or off only while the VM is stopped.
vmForm.guestWatchSecsHint: 30–3600 seconds. Shorter recovers faster but may restart a guest that is only briefly busy.
vmForm.pinnedHint: Automatic load balancing (the balancer) won't move this VM. HA recovery, node evacuation and manual moves still work.
vmForm.maxVcpusHint: (Advanced) Reserves room to add vCPUs up to this number while the VM runs. Empty means none. Applies from the next start.
vmForm.maxMemoryHint: (Advanced) Lets you grow memory up to this size while the VM runs (Linux guests). Empty means none. Applies from the next start.
vmForm.liveHint: vCPU cores and memory within the maximums apply right away where the node supports it. Other CPU, memory, firmware and machine changes apply at the next restart.
vmForm.runningNoteLive: The VM is running and its node cannot change. Hardware changes are applied while it runs where possible; the rest are listed on its page and apply at the next restart.
vmForm.restartForHotplug: This VM was started without room for adding devices. Restart it once to attach or detach disks and interfaces while running.
vmForm.disksLive: While running you can add disks at the end (virtio-blk only, up to 8) and remove disks added while running, from the end. Disks present at start can't change.
vmForm.nicsLive: While the VM runs, interfaces can be added at the end (8 devices at most) and interfaces added while it runs can be removed from the end. The network, model and MAC address of a running interface cannot change; its security groups can.
vmForm.replicationNote: Copies disks on node-local pools to other nodes on a schedule. If the VM's node fails, HA starts it there from the latest copy. Can't be combined with snapshots.
vmForm.haNoReplica: This VM cannot be restarted on another node: disk {{volume}} is on node-local pool {{pool}} and has no replica. Add replication.

vmForm.bootOrderRunning: Stop the VM to change the boot order.
vmForm.ciEnabled: Set up the guest on first boot (cloud-init)

vmForm.ciUserHint: Renames the distribution's default user. Empty keeps its name.

vmForm.ciKeysHint: One key per line (ssh-ed25519, ssh-rsa, ecdsa-sha2-…).
vmForm.ciUserDataHint: Used as it is instead of the generated user-data (start with #cloud-config).
vmForm.ciVendorDataHint: Runs together with the generated user-data, for packages and runcmd.
vmForm.ciUserDataWarning: The user-data replaces the generated user-data; user, password and SSH keys are not used.
vmForm.securityLive: TPM changes apply at the next restart. Secure Boot can only change while the VM is stopped.
vmForm.tpmHint: Virtual TPM chip (swtpm), needed by Windows 11 and BitLocker. Its state follows the VM between nodes.
vmForm.secureBootHint: UEFI feature (with Microsoft keys) that boots only signed boot loaders. Recommended for Windows 11; unsigned OSes won't boot.

vmForm.secureBootRunning: Stop the VM to change Secure Boot.
vmForm.secureBootReset: The VM already has UEFI variables. Change Secure Boot with "Reset firmware" on the VM page.

haChecks.pageHint: Every node checks these links, ping targets and storage pool paths every 5 seconds and sends the results with its heartbeat. When a check fails on a node for longer than the wait time, the reaction set below runs. If many nodes fail together, it is treated as a shared failure and only warns.
haChecks.autoNote: Each node also checks its cluster links by itself (cluster-link-1, cluster-link-2 …). Those checks only warn and are shown with the node.
haChecks.graceHint: The check must keep failing this long before anything happens. Default 10 (10–600). Longer ignores short blips but recovers later.
haChecks.overridesHint: A different target on some nodes, such as another interface name. Other nodes use the target above.

roleHint.management: The network used to manage the node. VMs can keep running without it, so by default it only warns.
roleHint.storage: Whether the node reaches the shared storage holding VM disks. If not, VMs using those disks are started again on another node.
roleHint.vm: A network VMs use. If it fails, VMs on it are moved to another node while running (live migration).

kindHint.link: Passes while the interface has a link. For a bond, losing some ports only shows as degraded; losing all fails.
kindHint.ping: Pings each address once (2 seconds); passes when at least Need addresses answer. Via picks the interface (Linux only).
kindHint.pool: Reads a small file on the pool (NFS, shared directory), checks the iSCSI sessions and multipath paths (shared LVM) or asks the Ceph OSDs (RBD).

kindHint.soft-node-anti-affinity: Avoids the chosen nodes; a chosen node adds the weight.

placement.pageHint: Every node sends its load (1- and 5-minute CPU, memory) with its heartbeat every 5 seconds. VM start, HA recovery and node evacuation pick the node with the best score. Every 5 minutes the balancer looks at the load difference between nodes and suggests or makes live migrations.

modeHint.recommend: The balancer only recommends moves; apply them yourself.
modeHint.auto: The balancer starts up to two live migrations at a time by itself.

policyHint.pack: Fills busy nodes first and keeps others empty (to save power or for maintenance). The balancer only fixes broken 'hard' rules.

placement.thresholdHint: Suggest moves when the load difference between nodes is above this (1–50%). Default 15%. Smaller moves more often; larger waits for a bigger difference.

pausedReasons.pack: The policy is pack, so the balancer does not move VMs for balance.

memory.label: Host memory binding

subnets.none: No subnets: VMs get no address on this network.

When you add a subnet, interfaces that have no address get one from it (running guests pick it up at their next DHCP renewal); interfaces that already have an address keep it (fill a missing family with orbivisorctl network ips NAME --fill).

wizard.title: Set up SDN (OVN)
wizard.centralsHint: Choose 1, 3 or 5 central nodes that store and hand out the SDN settings (with 3, one can fail and SDN keeps working). The first is set up first and the others join one at a time. Packages are installed with apt.

sync.title: Last sync
sync.caughtUp: Every node has applied the latest settings.

centrals.title: Central nodes
centrals.hint: The nodes that store the SDN settings (1, 3 or 5). Changing them copies the data, so one change runs at a time.
centrals.removeDescription: An online node leaves the settings databases and stops its central role (its files are renamed, not deleted); it stays a node connector (chassis). An offline node is removed from the databases by another central node instead.
centrals.addDescription: Installs the SDN central packages on the node with apt and joins it to the settings databases.

sdn.noNodes: No other node can become a central.

move.hint: The setup stopped on {{node}}, which is offline or gone, before any central was up. Move the setup to another node.

sdn.serverChecks: The server checks that SDN (OVN) is set up when you create the network.

strays.hint: These nodes are not central nodes but may still be members of the settings database, which lowers how many failures it can survive. Remove them.

strays.gone: {{name}} was removed from the cluster but may still be an OVN database member.
strays.removeNamed: Remove the leftover central databases of {{name}}
strays.removeTitle: Remove the leftover OVN central databases of {{name}}?
strays.removeDescription: An online node leaves the databases and stops them (its files are renamed, not deleted). An offline or removed node is kicked out by a live central.

physnet.title: SDN physical networks
physnet.editDescription: Give physical network names to this node's Linux bridges, and choose whether this node can host routers' outside door (gateway).
physnet.name: Physical network
physnet.bridgeHint: The bridge must already exist on the node. Orbivisor only plugs into it and does not change its settings.
physnet.priorityHint: 1–1000. Higher takes over first; routers spread evenly across nodes with the same value.
physnet.gatewayPending: (the SDN agent has not applied it yet)
physnet.pickHint: The physical network name tied to a bridge on a node's page (Cluster & availability › Nodes › a node's SDN physical networks).
physnet.noneHint: No node has a physical network yet. Add one on a node's page first (Cluster & availability › Nodes › a node's SDN physical networks).
physnet.vlanHint: Optional, 1–4094. Empty plugs straight into the physical network untagged (flat).
physnet.mtuHint: 1280–9000. Empty means 1500 (same as the physical network). Raise it if the physical switches take jumbo frames.

errors.name: Use a lowercase letter, then up to 30 lowercase letters, digits or -.
errors.duplicate: This physical network is listed twice.
errors.bridge: Use the name of a Linux bridge (1–15 characters, not br-int).

lockdown.title: OVN access lockdown
lockdown.hint: Chassis can only change their own rows in the southbound database, only northd writes through the privileged port, and the OVN ports accept only the addresses of cluster members. A node removed from the cluster is cut off even though its certificate is still valid.
lockdown.turningOn: Turn on the OVN access lockdown
lockdown.turningOff: Turn off the OVN access lockdown
lockdown.checkSets: {{members}} member addresses and {{centrals}} central addresses will be allowed.
lockdown.noOutside: Nothing outside the allow list is connected to a central now.
lockdown.outside_one: {{count}} connection to a central comes from outside the allow list. It is cut off when the lockdown turns on (a member node behind NAT or a removed node).
lockdown.outside_other: {{count}} connections to centrals come from outside the allow list. They are cut off when the lockdown turns on (member nodes behind NAT or removed nodes).
lockdown.force: Turn on anyway (these connections are cut off)
lockdown.offTitle: Turn off the OVN access lockdown?
lockdown.offDescription: The allow lists come down first, then each central goes back to the plain ports. Any node with the cluster certificate can then write to the southbound database again.

text.twoCentrals: The cluster has two OVN centrals: while each one restarts its southbound database, the other alone is not a majority, so the southbound database is unavailable for a few seconds per central (the data path keeps working). Add a third central to avoid it.
text.raftCut: The address allow-list cut the OVN Raft connections and was removed again. Check first for Raft peers outside the central set.
text.notSwitched: The OVN central {{name}} did not switch its lockdown in {{secs}} s. Is it online, with the other centrals in quorum?
text.notKept: The OVN central {{name}} could not keep its address allow-list: it cut the OVN Raft connections.
text.notApplied: The OVN address allow-list is not applied on {{nodes}} yet; the SDN agent there keeps trying.
text.notRemoved: The OVN address allow-list is not removed on {{nodes}} yet; the SDN agent there keeps trying.
text.replaced: Another request changed the OVN lockdown; this task stopped.
text.offAgain: The lockdown was turned off again.

migration.title: Migrate {{name}} to SDN
migration.description: Moves the VM interfaces of this simple network to an SDN network, keeping their addresses. Each VM moves stopped, live (about a second without network) or with a restart; a temporary bridge connects both sides until you finish.
migration.createNew: A new SDN network with the same subnet
migration.cidrHint: The subnet of the source network, so the addresses stay.
migration.gatewayHint: The physical router's address: it stays the default route while the bridge is up.

modeHint.auto: Stopped VMs change in place; running VMs move live when they can, otherwise they restart.
modeHint.live: Running VMs move live (tap moved, about a second without network). VMs that can't are blocked.
modeHint.restart: Running VMs are shut down, changed and started again.
modeHint.offline: Only stopped VMs move. Running VMs are blocked.

migration.allowShrink: Move live even if the guest's MTU shrinks
migration.bridgeHint: Moved and remaining VMs stay on one L2 through a bridge (OVN l2gateway) on one node until you finish.
migration.bridgeNodeAuto: Automatic (the node with the most VMs)
migration.planHint: Nothing has changed yet. Fix an address, leave a VM out or change the mode, then plan again. Blocked VMs are skipped.
migration.instanceIdBanner: Some VMs use first-boot setup (cloud-init): their instance-id changes, so on next start the guest repeats its first-boot steps (SSH host keys and the like).
migration.noNics: No VM has an interface on this network.
migration.newBridgeNodeHint: The bridge node was removed from the cluster. Pick another node to resume.
migration.rollbackDescription: The VMs go back to the source network with their security groups and cloud-init addresses; running VMs move live (or restart if the MTU would shrink). The bridge comes down when the last VM is back.
migration.finishHint: Finishing removes the bridge. You can attach {{target}} to a router at the same time so the router becomes the default gateway.
migration.finishLeft_one: {{count}} interface is still on the source network.
migration.finishLeft_other: {{count}} interfaces are still on the source network.
migration.routerHint: The router port takes the subnet gateway address: DHCP guests switch at the next renewal, static guests right away.
migration.deleteDescription: The migration stops where it is and its bridge comes down. Moved VMs stay on the SDN network.
migration.deleteRecordDescription: Only the record goes away. The VMs stay as they are.

backupStores.pageHint: Backup stores that keep each identical piece once, in a backup pool or an S3-compatible bucket, optionally encrypted on the nodes. Back up to a store from the Backups tab of a VM or from a backup schedule.

empty.title: No backup stores
empty.description: A backup store cuts VM disks into 4 MiB pieces, keeps each identical piece once, verifies them on a schedule and can encrypt them before they leave the node.

backupStores.deleteDescription: Only the store resource is removed. The data in the bucket or directory stays; remove it by hand. A store that still has backups cannot be deleted.
backupStores.createDescription: Choose where the pieces go, whether they are encrypted, and when space cleanup and verification run.
backupStores.created: Backup store {{name}} created. It is being initialized.
backupStores.poolHint: A directory or NFS pool that stores backups. The store lives in store/<id> inside the pool.
backupStores.endpointHint: An https:// URL, such as https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com or your MinIO address.
backupStores.prefixHint: A folder inside the bucket, such as orbivisor/. Leave empty to use the whole bucket.
backupStores.secretHint: Kept in the cluster database only. It is never shown again.
backupStores.caHint: PEM of the CA that signed the endpoint certificate. Leave empty to trust the system roots.
backupStores.readOnlyHint: Opens a store another cluster owns, to restore from it (disaster recovery). Backups, deletes and cleanup are blocked; Scan adds its backups here.
backupStores.storeIdHint: The directory name under store/ in the pool, written by the cluster that made the store.

encryptHint.none: Pieces are only compressed. Whoever can read the store can read the backups.
encryptHint.generate: Pieces, VM settings and firmware state are encrypted with AES-256-GCM on the node. You get a recovery key once, right after creating the store.
encryptHint.recovery: Opens or creates a store with an existing key, such as a copy of another store.
encryptHint.escrow: Opens a store whose key was wrapped with a passphrase inside the store.

backupStores.recoveryKeyHint: The OPK1-… key printed when the store was created.
backupStores.unlockHint: The passphrase given when the key was escrowed.
backupStores.escrowHint: Also wraps the key with this passphrase inside the store, so the store can be opened without this cluster. At least 8 characters. The passphrase is not saved.
backupStores.scheduleHint: Times are UTC. Space cleanup removes pieces no backup uses any more; verification re-reads pieces and checks them.
backupStores.reverifyHint: Backups verified longer ago than this are verified again.

mode.full: Full (read all of the backup's pieces)

backupStores.verifyNew: Verify each new backup right after it is made

errors.exists: A backup store with this name already exists.
errors.endpoint: Enter an https:// URL with only a host and an optional port.
errors.bucket: Enter a bucket of 3-63 lowercase letters, digits, dots and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit.
errors.region: Enter a region of 1-32 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.
errors.prefix: Enter a path of up to 512 characters with no leading /, and no empty, . or .. parts.
errors.caPem: Paste a PEM certificate (BEGIN CERTIFICATE) of at most 64 KiB.
errors.accessKeyId: Enter the access key ID: 1-128 characters with no spaces.
errors.secretKey: Enter the secret access key: 1-256 characters with no spaces or line breaks.
errors.recoveryKey: Enter a recovery key that starts with OPK1-.
errors.reverifyDays: Enter a number of days from 1 to 3650.
errors.credentials: Give both the access key ID and the secret access key, or neither.

key.recoveryWarning: Store this key now, away from the cluster. Without it the backups cannot be recovered if the cluster is lost.
key.qr: Recovery key of {{name}} as a QR code
key.printBlocked: The print window was blocked. Allow pop-ups, or copy the key.
key.saved: I have stored the recovery key
key.confirmFirst: Confirm that you have stored the recovery key before closing. It is shown only now.
key.title: Key
key.adminOnly: Only cluster administrators can show the recovery key or escrow it.
key.exportDescription: The recovery key opens every backup in this store. Showing it is recorded in the audit log.
key.exportShown: Store it away from the cluster. Showing it was recorded in the audit log.
key.escrowed: The key of {{name}} is escrowed in the store.
key.escrowDescription: Wraps the key with a passphrase (Argon2id) and writes it into the store, replacing an earlier escrow. With the store and the passphrase the backups can be opened without this cluster. The passphrase is not saved.

backupStores.checkOk: This node read the store and the key matches.
backupStores.checkNotHere: This node cannot use the store (it is in another node's local pool). Below are the nodes' own reports.
backupStores.noReports: No node has reported on this store yet.
backupStores.takeOverDescription: This cluster becomes the owner of the store and may write to it. Cluster {{owner}} must not use it any more: two clusters writing one store can delete each other's backups.
backupStores.takeOverForce: Take over even if the owner was active in the last 24 hours
backupStores.settingsDescription: The backend and the encryption cannot be changed.
backupStores.credentialsHint: Leave both empty to keep the current credentials.

liveRestore.switchHint: Starts the new VM before its disks are copied.
liveRestore.switchOnHint: The VM starts in seconds and reads blocks it does not have yet from the backup while the disks are copied in the background; then it switches to the new disks. Until then it cannot be stopped normally, migrated, snapshotted or backed up, and HA protects it only afterwards. It runs on a node that reaches the backup.
liveRestore.dialogDescription: Makes a new VM from the backup and starts it right away. Its disks are filled from the backup in the background.
liveRestore.title: Live restore
liveRestore.waiting: Waiting for the copy to start
liveRestore.hint: Stopping, migrating, snapshots, backups and disk changes wait until the restore finishes. Force stop keeps what was copied; starting the VM again continues.
liveRestore.cancelDescription: The VM is stopped and deleted with its new disks. Everything the guest wrote since it started is discarded.
liveRestore.blockedBackup: The VM is being live-restored. Back it up when the restore has finished.

fileRestore.title: Files in {{name}}
fileRestore.idleHint: The helper VM stops after a while without browsing, downloads or restores. Leaving this page keeps it open; come back to use it again.
fileRestore.slowNode: Slow node (no hardware acceleration): up to a minute
fileRestore.booting: Starting a helper VM to read the backup ({{time}})
fileRestore.bootingHint: The backup is attached read-only to a small isolated VM. This usually takes a few seconds.
fileRestore.bootingSlowHint: The backup is attached read-only to a small isolated VM. This node has no hardware acceleration, so it can take up to a minute.
fileRestore.unusable: This browsing session cannot be used
fileRestore.nothingToBrowseHint: The disks in this backup have no supported filesystem. The list on the left says why for each one.
fileRestore.unreachable: Cannot reach the node of this session right now. Retrying…
fileRestore.waitingForNode: Waiting for the node to answer…
fileRestore.noVolumes: No disks found in the backup.

blocked.lvm: LVM physical volume — browse its logical volumes

fileRestore.filterLoaded: The filter only sees the names loaded so far. Load more to search further.
fileRestore.selectedHidden_one: (+{{count}} hidden by the filter, not included)
fileRestore.selectedHidden_other: (+{{count}} hidden by the filter, not included)
fileRestore.rawNameHint: This name is not valid UTF-8. Unknown bytes are shown as �; downloads keep the original bytes.
fileRestore.keys: Keys: ↑/↓ move, Enter opens a folder, Backspace goes up, Space selects.
fileRestore.downloadStartedArchive: Download started. If items are skipped or the archive stops early, {{report}} at the top of the archive says why.
fileRestore.tooMany: Select at most {{max}} items, or clear the selection to download the whole folder.
fileRestore.toVmDescription: Writes the selected files into a running VM through its guest agent. Owners, modes and times are not restored.
fileRestore.noRunningVms: No running VM that you may change has a guest agent channel. Turn on the guest agent of a VM and start it.
fileRestore.checkingAgent: Asking the guest agent what it allows…
fileRestore.noFileWrite: The guest agent does not allow writing files. {{reason}}
fileRestore.noMkdir: The selection has folders, but the guest agent does not allow running commands, which creating folders needs. Select files only, or allow guest-exec. {{reason}}
fileRestore.overwriteNeedsExec: Needs guest-exec, which the agent does not allow. {{reason}}
fileRestore.targetDirHint: The selected items are placed in this folder. It is created if it does not exist.
fileRestore.dirLinux: Use an absolute path that starts with /.

conflictHints.keep: Write the restored file next to it as name.restored-<time>.
conflictHints.skip: Leave the existing file and do not write the restored one.
conflictHints.overwrite: Replace the existing file (written to a temporary name first).

fileRestore.toVmLimits: Writing through the guest agent is slow (about 1–3 MB/s). The node limits how many files and bytes one restore can write. Follow the progress in Tasks.

errors.file_restore_busy: Too many browsing sessions or downloads are running. Try again in a moment. {{message}}
errors.file_restore_unavailable: No node can open this backup: {{message}}
errors.session_closed: The browsing session is closed. Open the backup again.
errors.session_not_ready: The helper VM is still starting.
errors.session_not_found: This browsing session no longer exists (the node may have restarted). Open the backup again.
errors.entry_not_found: The file or folder was not found in the backup.
errors.link_expired: The download link expired. Start the download again.
errors.file_restore_timeout: The helper VM did not answer in time. Try again.
errors.invalid_target_dir: The folder in the guest is not valid: {{message}}
errors.guest_mkdir_unavailable: Creating folders needs guest-exec, which the guest agent does not allow. Select files only.
errors.guest_overwrite_unavailable: Overwriting needs guest-exec, which the guest agent does not allow. Choose Keep both or Skip.
errors.guest_agent_restricted: The guest agent blocks file writes: {{message}}
errors.volume_not_found: This volume is no longer in the session. Open the backup again.

pools.intro: Where VM disks (volumes) and backups are kept. A 'local' pool is separate on each node; a 'shared' pool is used by all nodes. VMs on shared pools move between nodes quickly and HA can restart them anywhere (on local pools, only where a replica exists).
pools.empty: To create VMs you need a pool for their disks. The simplest is a folder (directory) on each node.
pools.name: The name screens and VM settings use for this pool. Lowercase letters, digits and - only (not at the start or end); it cannot be changed later.
pools.vg: An LVM volume group that already exists on the nodes (check with `vgs`).
pools.thinpool: The LVM area that only takes the space VMs actually write. In `lvs`, its attributes start with 'twi'.
pools.sharedVg: The shared volume group on a LUN every node sees (check with `vgs`).
pools.dataset: A ZFS dataset that already exists on the nodes (e.g. tank/opl, see `zfs list`). VM disks become zvols under it.
pools.cephPool: An RBD pool that already exists in Ceph. With Orbivisor-managed Ceph, use a pool made on the Ceph page.
pools.namespace: Separates names when several clusters share one Ceph pool. Usually left empty.

cluster.intro: The nodes in this cluster and their roles. To add a server, issue a join token to get a join command, then run it on the new server.
cluster.ttl: Run the join command on the new node within this time. Default 1 hour — shorter is safer when you join right away.

nodes.intro: The servers (nodes) in the cluster. Open a row for its metrics, CPU and VMs; use the ⋯ menu for maintenance (move VMs off), labels and removal. To add a node, issue a join token on the Cluster page.

fence.address: The address of the node's remote management card (BMC, iDRAC, iLO), such as 10.0.0.101 — the card's IP, not the node OS.
fence.user: The management card user. It must be allowed to power the server on and off.
fence.password: The management card user's password. It is not shown again after saving.
fence.url: The Redfish address of the management card, such as https://10.0.0.101
fence.caPem: The CA (PEM) that signed the management card's certificate. Empty accepts only certificates the system trusts.

networks.intro: Networks are what VM network cards plug into. A 'bridge' network on a node's existing bridge is the simplest (administrators only); with several nodes, pick 'VXLAN' or 'SDN' so a VM sees the same network on any node.
networks.empty: VMs can already reach the outside through the user network (NAT). Create a network so VMs can talk to each other or to your LAN.
networks.name: The name you pick in a VM's network card settings. 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end).
networks.bridge: A Linux bridge already set up on the nodes, such as vmbr0. VMs on this network only start on nodes that have it.

backups.intro: Backups of every VM, including VMs that were deleted. Make one now from the VM's Backups tab, or let a backup schedule make them automatically.
backups.empty: Press 'Back up now' on a VM's Backups tab, or create a backup schedule to back up automatically at a set time.
backups.vmEmpty: This VM has no backups yet. Back it up now or add it to a backup schedule.
backups.pool: The storage pool that holds the backup files. A pool on another disk or a NAS keeps backups even if the node's disk fails.
backups.restoreName: The name of the new VM made from the backup. Use another name while the original VM still exists.
backups.restorePool: Where the new VM's disks go. A shared pool allows HA and fast migration.
backups.restoreNetwork: The network of this cluster to use instead of the one the backed-up VM was on.
backups.restoreSecurityGroup: The security group to use instead of one this cluster does not have. Its rules apply to the new VM.
backups.convertStore: The backup store to copy this backup into. The original backup stays. A store keeps each identical piece only once, saving space.
backups.copyStore: Another backup store to hold a copy, such as S3 in addition to a fast local store.
backups.replicateRemote: Another Orbivisor cluster that receives the copy, so you can restore there if this site is lost.
backups.remotePool: The backup pool on the remote cluster that holds the copy.
backups.remoteStore: The backup store on the remote cluster that holds the copy. Only pieces it does not have are sent.

backupJobs.intro: Backs up the chosen VMs automatically on the chosen days and time, and deletes this schedule's backups that the retention rules (last n, daily, weekly, monthly) do not keep. Times are UTC; each node runs at most 2 backups at once.
backupJobs.empty: Create a backup schedule to back up VMs automatically at a set time, such as every night, and delete old ones.
backupJobs.name: The name of this schedule in lists, such as nightly-prod. It cannot be changed later.
backupJobs.target: Which VMs this schedule backs up. Choosing by label also picks up VMs that get the same label later.

settings.intro: Settings that apply to the whole cluster at once: where updates come from, what happens on host shutdown and HA, the VM CPU baseline, usage reports and metrics export. Only administrators can change them.

haAmount.nodes: How many nodes may die at once. That much memory, starting with the largest nodes, is kept free. Usually 1.
haAmount.percent: The share of all HA node memory kept free. For example with 4 nodes, 25% is one node's worth.

subscription.intro: A subscription key unlocks the enterprise update channel and support. Every feature works without one.

sdn.intro: Builds virtual switches and routers across the nodes, so a VM keeps the same private network on any node. (Similar to VMware NSX.)
sdn.chassis: A connector program that runs on each node where SDN VMs start. SDN VMs only start on nodes marked ready.
sdn.moveNode: The node that takes over the first setup. Pick one that is online and can install the SDN packages.
sdn.centralNode: A node that shares the job of storing and handing out the SDN settings. Add them one at a time to reach 1, 3 or 5.
sdn.cidr: The address range of this network, such as 10.10.0.0/24 (gateway 10.10.0.1, VMs .2–.254). It cannot change once saved.
sdn.gatewaySaved: The gateway of a saved subnet cannot change. To change it, remove the subnet and add it again.
sdn.subnetDescription: Optional. A note on what this address range is for (up to 200 characters).
sdn.dhcp: On: VMs get the address Orbivisor assigned automatically when they start. Off: the VM must still use that address (shown on the VM page) — traffic from other addresses is blocked (cloud-init sets it for you).
sdn.physnetName: The name SDN uses for this physical network, such as ext. You pick it when creating an external network.
sdn.physnetBridge: The Linux bridge on this node that reaches that physical network, such as vmbr1. It may differ per node.
sdn.gateway: On: this node can host a router's external gateway. Turn it on only on nodes that reach the outside network.

backupStores.intro: A backup store keeps identical content only once. Backups are cut into pieces and each identical piece is stored once; cleanup removes pieces no backup uses to give the space back.
backupStores.name: The name screens and backup schedules use for this store. Lowercase letters, digits and - only (not at the start or end).
backupStores.backend: Where the pieces are actually kept: a backup pool (a folder or NFS on the nodes) or an S3-compatible bucket (AWS S3, MinIO and so on).
backupStores.region: The region of the bucket, such as us-east-1. Without regions (like MinIO), us-east-1 usually works.
backupStores.bucket: The S3 bucket that holds the pieces. Create it first.
backupStores.accessKeyId: The access key ID of an S3 user that can read, write, list and delete objects in the bucket (without delete, cleanup fails and space keeps growing).
backupStores.verifyMode: Full re-reads every piece the checked backups use, to find damage (slow). Metadata only checks those pieces exist (fast).
backupStores.gcAt: When the space cleanup starts (UTC, HH:MM). Pick a time with few backups running, such as 05:00.
backupStores.escrowPassphrase: The passphrase that wraps the key (8+ characters). With the store and this passphrase you can open the backups even without this cluster.
backupStores.passphraseAgain: Type the same passphrase again to catch typos.

images.intro: Cloud images of well-known Linux distributions. Download (⬇) puts one in a pool as a disk and can also make a template you can stamp VMs from right away.
images.empty: There are no images to download. An administrator can add in-house images to the list.
images.pool: The storage pool for the downloaded disk. For a template used on several nodes, a shared pool (NFS, Ceph) is best.
images.volumeName: The name of the downloaded disk (volume). Empty uses the suggested name shown in grey.
images.makeTemplate: When on, a stopped template VM is made from the disk after the download. VMs can be cloned from a template in seconds.
images.templateName: The name of the template VM. You pick it by this name in Templates and when creating VMs.
images.network: The network the template's network card joins. Cloned VMs start on it too.
images.cpus: Number of virtual CPUs. 2 by default; clones can change it.
images.memory: Memory size. 2048 MiB (2 GiB) by default.
images.size: Cannot be smaller than the image. It can grow later but never shrink. Empty keeps the image size.

add.title: The name shown in the list (e.g. Corp Ubuntu 24.04).
add.os: The distribution name (e.g. ubuntu), used to filter the list.
add.url: The http or https address the nodes download the image from. The nodes must be able to reach it.
add.arch: The CPU type of the image. It must match the nodes for the VM to start.
add.firmware: How the image boots. Modern cloud images mostly use UEFI, older ones BIOS.
add.format: The format of the downloaded file. Cloud images are usually qcow2.
add.checksumKind: How to check that the downloaded file is not broken or tampered with. Pick the checksum file when the publisher has one.
add.sumsUrl: The address of the publisher's checksum file (e.g. …/SHA256SUMS). The node finds the image's hash in it.
add.digest: The image hash (hex) the publisher announced. The download fails if the file does not match.
add.defaultUser: The login user built into the image (e.g. ubuntu). Used as the default when making a template.
add.minSize: The size of the image's disk. Template disks cannot be made smaller than this.

isos.intro: ISO files for installing operating systems. Upload one or download it from a URL, then put it in a VM's CD-ROM to install.
isos.empty: You need an ISO file to install an OS. Upload one from your computer or download it straight from the publisher's URL.

downloads.url: The http or https address of the file. A node that uses the pool must reach it directly.
downloads.name: The name for the downloaded file. Filled in from the URL's file name.
downloads.pool: The storage pool for the file. A shared pool is best when VMs on several nodes will use it.
downloads.sourceFormat: The format of the file being downloaded. VMware disks are vmdk.
downloads.format: The format kept in the pool. qcow2 takes only what is written and supports snapshots; raw is a little faster.

uploads.file: The file on your computer. It goes to the node you are connected to.
uploads.name: The name for the uploaded file. Filled in from the file name.
uploads.pool: The storage pool for the file. Only pools usable on the node you are connected to are listed.
uploads.sourceFormat: The format of the file. VMware disks are vmdk; cloud images are usually qcow2.

imports.intro: Bring VMs from VMware into Orbivisor, from an OVA file or straight from ESXi or vCenter. Review the proposed settings and run it to get a stopped VM.
imports.empty: To bring a VMware VM over, upload an OVA file or connect to ESXi.
imports.ovaFile: An .ova file exported from VMware. It goes to the node you are connected to.
imports.ovaName: The name of this import. Filled in from the file name.
imports.vmName: The name of the VM to create. It must not clash with another VM.
imports.sockets: Number of virtual CPU sockets. Keeping the source value is safest.
imports.cores: Cores per socket. Sockets × cores is the VM's vCPU count.
imports.memory: The VM's memory (MiB), taken from the source VM.
imports.firmware: How the source VM booted. Changing it may stop the VM from booting; keep the source value.
imports.diskBus: How disks are attached. Keep the suggestion made for the source OS: virtio-blk is fast but the guest needs its driver (most Linux has it); SATA works without drivers (suggested for Windows). A Windows guest without the driver does not boot on virtio-blk.
imports.nicModel: The network card type. Keep the suggestion: virtio is fast but needs a guest driver (most Linux has it); e1000e works without drivers (suggested for Windows).
imports.network: Choose which Orbivisor network the card on this source network joins.
imports.esxiHost: The name or IP address of the ESXi host or vCenter.
imports.esxiUser: The VMware user to log in as (e.g. root, administrator@vsphere.local).
imports.esxiPassword: That user's password. It is kept only in the memory of the node running the import, never stored.
imports.esxiName: The name of this import. Filled in from the chosen VM's name.

volumes.intro: The VM disks (volumes). Create an empty disk, upload or download an image as a disk, grow disks or delete them.
volumes.empty: There are no disks yet. Creating a VM creates its disk, and you can also create an empty disk here.
volumes.name: The name of the disk. VM settings attach it by this name.
volumes.pool: The storage pool for the disk. On a shared pool the VM moves to other nodes quickly.
volumes.size: The disk size the VM sees. A qcow2 disk only takes what is written. It can only grow later.
volumes.format: qcow2: takes only what is written, supports snapshots (recommended). raw: one plain file, a little faster, but no snapshots on directory and NFS pools.
volumes.newSize: Only a larger size works. Grow the partition inside the guest afterwards.

ceph.intro: Orbivisor sets up Ceph itself: spare disks on 3 or more nodes become one storage that every node uses. To use an existing Ceph, create a Ceph RBD pool under Storage pools.
ceph.initNode: The node for the first monitor and manager. Any node works; the others are added in the next steps.
ceph.monNode: The node for the new monitor. Three monitors (an odd number) on different nodes keep Ceph running when one node is down.
ceph.mgrNode: The node for a standby manager. It takes over when the active manager's node goes down.
ceph.osdNode: The node that gives a disk to Ceph. Choose one of its empty disks below.
ceph.poolName: The name this pool goes by in Storage pools and VM disks.
ceph.size: How many copies of the data are kept. 3 is recommended; copies are always on different nodes.

routers.intro: A router joins SDN private networks to each other and, through an external network, lets private VMs reach the internet (SNAT). To let the outside reach a VM, attach a floating IP (external address).
routers.name: The name of this router. 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end).
routers.description: Optional. A note on what this router joins (up to 200 characters).
routers.snat: On: private VMs share the router's one outside address to reach the internet. Usually leave it on.
routers.addInterface: An SDN network to attach to this router. Its VMs then go through the router to other networks and the outside.
routers.destination: The address range to send along this route, such as 10.20.0.0/16.
routers.nexthop: The address of the next device toward that destination. It must be on a network the router is attached to, such as 10.10.0.254.

remotes.intro: Orbivisor clusters at other sites, and the backup schedules that send copies there. If this whole site is lost, you can restore on the remote cluster.
remotes.empty: Register an Orbivisor cluster at another site to send backup copies there. If this cluster is the standby site, register the main site and use a DR plan to bring its VMs back up here.
remotes.name: The name this cluster uses for the remote cluster, such as dr-site. It cannot be changed later.

fip.intro: A floating IP (external address) ties one address of an external network to one private VM, so the outside can reach that VM directly (for example, to publish a web server). A private-range address on the external network works too.
fip.network: The external network to take the address from: a free one from its floating IP ranges.

alerts.intro: When something goes wrong — CPU stays high, a node goes down — an alert fires and a notification goes where you chose (email, Slack and more). Rules decide what to watch; notification targets decide where to send.
alerts.empty: No alerts are firing now. When a problem matches a rule, it shows up here.
alerts.historyEmpty: Use Test on a notification target to check that notifications really arrive.

alertRules.empty: A rule watches a condition such as "node CPU above 90% for 5 minutes" and sends a notification.
alertRules.name: The name of this rule (for example node-cpu-high). Lowercase letters, digits and - (not at the start or end); it cannot change later.
alertRules.condition: What to watch. States (a value over a threshold, or something that lasts, such as a node being down — can have a duration) or events (something that happens once, such as a task failing or an HA recovery — no duration).
alertRules.value: The value that triggers the alert.
alertRules.percent: Notify when the pool is this full. 80–90 is usual.
alertRules.role: Which ports to watch for a lost link. Default: uplink, underlay and service ports with addresses, plus bridges an administrator took down.
alertRules.severity: How serious the alert is. Critical: fix now; warning: will become a problem; info: good to know.
alertRules.sendResolved: Also sends one notification when the problem clears.

notificationTargets.intro: Where alert notifications go (email, Slack, Teams, a webhook and more). After creating one, press Test to check it arrives, then choose its name in an alert rule.
notificationTargets.empty: Alerts reach email or chat only through a notification target. Create one place to receive them.
notificationTargets.kind: How to send. Email (SMTP) or webhook (Slack, Teams, ntfy, Gotify or your own server).
notificationTargets.name: The name alert rules choose (for example ops-mail). Lowercase letters, digits and - (not at the start or end); it cannot change later.
notificationTargets.host: The SMTP server that sends the mail (for example smtp.example.com).
notificationTargets.port: The SMTP port. Usually 587 for STARTTLS and 465 for TLS.
notificationTargets.tls: How the connection to the server is encrypted. Follow your server's instructions — usually STARTTLS.
notificationTargets.password: The SMTP sign-in password. It is not shown again after saving.
notificationTargets.from: The sender address of the mail (for example orbivisor@example.com).
notificationTargets.format: The message shape the receiver expects. For Slack or Teams, use the incoming webhook URL from that app.
notificationTargets.token: The ntfy or Gotify access token. It is not shown again after saving.
notificationTargets.headers: Add only when the receiving server needs an auth header (such as Authorization). Values are not shown again after saving.

securityGroups.intro: Security groups are bundles of firewall rules. Put one on a VM network card and incoming traffic is accepted only when a rule allows it, while outgoing traffic is sent unless a rule drops it. Running VMs pick it up right away.
securityGroups.empty: To open only SSH (22) and web (443) on a VM and block the rest, create a rule bundle and put it on the VM's network card.
securityGroups.rulesEmpty: Cards with this group now drop all new incoming connections and send all outgoing traffic. Add rules for what to let in.
securityGroups.name: The name you pick in a VM's network card settings, such as web or ssh. 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end).
securityGroups.description: Optional. A note on what this group opens (up to 200 characters).

fileRestore.vm: The running VM to write the files back into. Its guest agent must be on; usually the original VM.

vms.intro: Every virtual machine (VM) in the cluster. Click a name for its state, console, snapshots and backups; use Create at the top right for a new VM.
vms.empty: Create a VM from scratch, or copy a ready-made template in seconds.
vms.cpu: Virtual CPU layout (sockets × cores) and CPU model. The host model passes the node's CPU through — fastest, but hard to move live to a node with a different CPU.
vms.vcpus: Number of virtual CPUs. If a maximum is shown, you can add vCPUs up to it while the VM runs.
vms.memory: Memory given to the VM. If a maximum is shown, you can grow it up to that while the VM runs.
vms.hotplug: Free slots for adding disks or network devices without turning the VM off. Only virtio disks can be added while it runs. If none, restart the VM once first.
vms.bootOrder: Devices the VM tries in turn when it starts. After installing the OS, the disk should come first.
vms.cloudInit: Settings put into the guest automatically on first boot — host name, user, SSH keys, addresses (cloud-init).
vms.template: This VM is a template: it can't be started, you deploy new VMs from it. The number counts linked clones built on it.
vms.linkedClone: This VM's disk stores only its changes on top of a template disk (linked clone), so the base disk can't be deleted.
vms.firmware: Firmware that boots the VM: UEFI (default for modern OSes) or BIOS (older OSes).
vms.machine: (Advanced) Virtual motherboard type: q35 on x86 nodes, virt on ARM nodes.
vms.restart: Whether Orbivisor restarts the VM when it stops with an error.
vms.power: Whether Orbivisor keeps this VM on or off. After a node reboots, it brings the VM back to this state.
vms.lastError: The last error while starting or running the VM. Fix the cause, then start it again.
vms.haPolicy: Whether the VM is restarted automatically on another node if its node fails (HA). The line below is how many restarts and moves are allowed within 10 minutes.
vms.haGroup: Set of nodes HA picks from when restarting this VM. Without one, any node is used.
vms.haPriority: Order when many VMs recover at once (0–100, higher first).
vms.guestWatch: For VMs with automatic recovery (HA) on: if the guest OS hangs and the guest agent doesn't answer for this long, the VM is force-restarted.
vms.pinned: Automatic load balancing won't move this VM. HA recovery and node evacuation still do.
vms.ruleViolations: Placement rules (keep together / keep apart) this VM doesn't meet right now — usually because resources forced it onto another node.
vms.haError: Why HA couldn't restart or move this VM. It clears when you fix the cause and start the VM again.

guest.settings: Guest agent settings: whether file systems are frozen for snapshots and backups, and how the VM is shut down.
guest.addresses: Network addresses of the guest. Shown only when the guest agent runs.
guest.user: Account inside the guest whose password to change (e.g. root, Administrator).
guest.newPassword: The guest agent changes it right away. Orbivisor does not store the password.
guest.passwordAgain: Type the same password again to catch typos.

security.tpm: Virtual TPM chip, needed by Windows 11 and BitLocker. Its state (keys) is stored on the node shown.
security.secureBoot: UEFI feature that only boots signed boot loaders. Recommended for Windows 11.
security.uefiVars: Where UEFI settings such as boot entries are kept. If booting gets stuck, clear them with Reset firmware.

vmForm.name: Name shown in lists and screens: 1–63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end). It can't be changed later.
vmForm.cores: Number of virtual CPUs. Start with 2 and add more if the VM is slow.
vmForm.memory: Memory for the VM in MiB (1024 = 1 GiB). 2048 is a good start for Linux servers, 4096 or more for Windows.
vmForm.firmware: Firmware that boots the VM. UEFI (default, recommended) for modern OSes; BIOS for old OSes or BIOS-only images.
vmForm.machine: (Advanced) Virtual motherboard type. Auto picks the right one for the node — usually leave it.
vmForm.node: Node the VM runs on. Auto picks a node with enough free resources.
vmForm.restart: Whether to restart the VM when it stops with an error. Pick 'On failure' for servers that should stay up.
vmForm.folder: Folder for the VM. It inherits the folder's permissions and quotas.
vmForm.agentShutdown: How Shut down works: a clean shutdown through the agent, falling back to the power-button signal (ACPI).
vmForm.scheduleKeep: How many scheduled snapshots to keep. Beyond that the oldest are deleted.

cpu.pinnedFlags: CPU features to add to or hide from the chosen model. Usually left empty.

migrate.node: Node to move the VM to. It pauses very briefly at the end. Disabled nodes can't run this VM's CPU.
migrate.pool: Pool on the target node for the copied node-local disks. By default, the pool with the same name.

clone.name: Name of the new VM: 1–63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end).
clone.source: What to copy. The current state works only for a stopped VM; pick a snapshot to copy a running VM as of that point.
clone.pool: Pool for the new disks. By default, the same pool as the source disks.

snapshots.name: A name to recognise the snapshot by (e.g. before-upgrade).
snapshots.description: Note what it was taken before, to find it later (optional).

templates.intro: A template is a VM master copy that can't be started. Deploying it creates a VM with the same setup in seconds; disks are linked clones that store only their changes.
templates.empty: Download an OS image from the image library as a template, or choose Convert to template from a stopped VM's menu.

deploy.count: How many VMs to create (1–100). For several, put {n} in the name.
deploy.first: First number for {n}. E.g. 1 gives web-1, web-2…
deploy.pool: Pool for the new disks. Keep the default (the template's pool) for fast linked clones.
deploy.memory: Empty keeps the template's value (MiB, 1024 = 1 GiB).
deploy.diskSize: Empty keeps the template's size. It can't be smaller than the template; you can grow it later but never shrink it.
deploy.nic: Network for this interface. Leave it to keep the template's network.

migration.target: SDN network to move the VM interfaces to. It needs the same subnet as the source so addresses stay.
migration.name: Name of the new SDN network.
migration.parallel: How many VMs to move at once. Higher is faster, but a problem then hits several VMs together. Start small.
migration.bridgeNode: Node that hosts the bridge joining both networks during the move. Traffic between the two sides passes through it.

haGroups.empty: HA works without groups. Create one when you want to set the order of nodes a VM goes to, such as 'databases on node1 first, then node2'. To keep VMs on those nodes only, turn on the group's 'Restricted'.
haGroups.name: The group name chosen in a VM's HA settings, such as db-nodes.

lb.intro: A load balancer spreads connections arriving at one address (VIP) over several VMs. Health checks take dead VMs out, so the service keeps running when one VM stops.
lb.name: The name of this load balancer. 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits or - (not at the start or end).
lb.description: Optional. A note on what it serves (up to 200 characters).
lb.listeners: A listener = 'spread connections to this VIP port over these members', such as TCP 443 → 3 web VMs.
lb.protocol: Usually TCP for web and databases, UDP for DNS or games.
lb.vipPort: The VIP port clients connect to, such as 443.
lb.health: On: members are probed regularly and get no traffic while they do not answer. Recommended.
lb.timeout: A check fails if there is no answer within this many seconds.
lb.rise: Back in after this many passes.
lb.memberIp: The member's IPv4 address, on an SDN network attached to the router. Devices other than VMs work too, but members given by address are not health-checked.
lb.memberPort: The port the member actually listens on.
lb.pickNic: Adds a VM network card on this router's networks as a member. It follows the VM if its address changes.

haChecks.intro: Every node checks its network and shared storage connections every 5 seconds. When a check fails on a node for longer than the wait time (10 seconds by default), only the HA VMs that check affects get its action (warn, move, or start elsewhere; management checks only warn by default). When most nodes fail together, it is treated as a shared fault and only warns.
haChecks.empty: Add HA checks so that, on a node that lost its switch or storage connection, the HA VMs the check affects are moved or restarted elsewhere (management checks only warn by default). A node that dies completely is handled by HA without any checks.
haChecks.name: The name of this check in lists, such as storage-nas or uplink-bond0.
haChecks.onFail: What to do when the check fails for longer than the wait time. Empty uses the default for what it checks.

topology.intro: See in one picture how networks, routers, floating IPs (external addresses), VMs and load balancers connect. Click an item to open it.
topology.folder: Draws only this folder's networks. Narrow it down when the picture is large.

users.intro: Users who can sign in to this cluster (local users, and directory users who have signed in at least once). The global role sets what they can do across the cluster; extra rights per folder or VM are set on the Permissions page.
users.empty: Create users so people other than the administrator can sign in as operators or viewers.
users.name: The name used to sign in (for example kim). It cannot change later.

tokens.intro: Keys that scripts and tools such as Terraform or Prometheus use instead of a password. A token has all of its creator's rights (global role plus folder and VM permissions), narrowed to its scope if you set one. Deleting it stops whatever uses it at once.
tokens.empty: Create an API token so scripts and other tools can manage this cluster. It is shown only once, when created.
tokens.name: A name that says where the token is used (for example terraform, prometheus).

account.intro: Set up two-factor sign-in: one more check after your password. Use a code from an authenticator app on your phone or a passkey (fingerprint, security key), and save the recovery codes in case you lose both.

security.intro: Choose who must use two-factor sign-in. Users with a chosen role, or in a chosen sign-in realm, must set it up at their next sign-in.

twoFactor.code: Enter the 6-digit number your authenticator app shows. It changes every 30 seconds.
twoFactor.passkeyName: A name to recognise this passkey (for example work laptop, YubiKey).
twoFactor.proofCode: Enter the 6-digit code from your authenticator app, or one of your saved recovery codes.
twoFactor.proofPassword: Without a code, confirm it is you with your sign-in password.

accounts.current: The password you use now, to confirm it is you.
accounts.confirm: Type the same password again to catch typos.

placementRules.intro: Rules for which nodes VMs run on. For example: the two web VMs on different nodes (so one survives a node failure), databases only on SSD nodes.
placementRules.empty: For example 'the two web VMs on different nodes' or 'databases only on SSD nodes'. Without rules, VMs go where the placement policy puts them (by default 'balance' — the least loaded node).
placementRules.name: The name of this rule in lists, such as web-spread or db-on-ssd.
placementRules.vmBy: Name the VMs the rule applies to, or pick them by label. With a label, VMs that get the same label later follow too.
placementRules.nodeBy: Pick nodes one by one or by node label (such as disk=ssd). Node labels are set on the Nodes page.

placement.intro: A VM's start node is picked by HA group priority, then 'if possible' rule penalties, then load (the least loaded node with the 'balance' policy, the fullest with 'pack'). Every 5 minutes the balancer looks at the load difference between nodes and, above the move threshold, suggests or makes VM moves.

realms.intro: Lets people sign in with company accounts (Active Directory, LDAP) or a sign-in service (OIDC — Keycloak, Azure AD, Google and others). Users become <name>@<realm>, and their role is set from their groups at every sign-in.
realms.empty: Without a realm, only the local users made here can sign in. Create one to let people sign in with company accounts.
realms.kind: LDAP: an in-house directory such as Active Directory or OpenLDAP. OIDC: a sign-in service such as Keycloak, Azure AD or Google (the browser goes there to sign in).
realms.name: The name after the user name (for example corp → kim@corp). local is reserved, and it cannot change later.
realms.clientId: The client ID you get when you register this cluster as an app in the IdP.
realms.usernameClaim: The token field used as the sign-in name. Usually preferred_username or email.
realms.baseDn: Where in the directory to start looking for users (for example dc=example,dc=com).
realms.bindPassword: The password of the service account above. It is not shown again after saving.
realms.groupAttr: The user attribute that lists their groups. Usually memberOf.
realms.timeout: If the directory or IdP does not answer in this time, the sign-in fails. 1–30 s.
realms.defaultRole: The role for users who match no group. None means they cannot sign in (recommended).
realms.testUser: The sign-in name of a directory user to test with (without the realm).
realms.testPassword: That user's password. Used only for the test, never saved.

permissions.intro: One table of who (users, groups) can do what (role) where (the whole cluster, a folder, one VM). Permissions only add up; nothing denies.
permissions.empty: Add permissions to give users and groups work per folder or VM, beyond their global role.
permissions.target: Where the permission applies. Choose a folder and turn on 'Apply inside the folder and its subfolders' to also cover the VMs, networks and storage in it.
permissions.principalKind: Give it to one person, or to a group of people. With many people, groups are easier.
permissions.principal: The user or group that gets the permission.
permissions.role: The set of things they can do there. You can only give roles within your own rights here.
permissions.propagate: On: the permission reaches everything in the folder (VMs, networks, storage) and its subfolders. Off: it applies to the folder itself only (renaming it and so on), not even to the VMs directly in it.

roles.intro: A role is a set of things someone can do (a privilege list). Besides the built-in roles (administrator, operator, viewer), make roles such as "backups only" and give them on the Permissions page.
roles.empty: Create a role to hand out just the work needed, such as "takes snapshots only".
roles.name: The name you pick on the Permissions page (for example backup-operator). admin, operator, viewer and none are reserved.
roles.description: A short note on what the role is for. It shows in the list.

groups.intro: A group is a set of people you give permissions to at once. Add local users directly, or link a company directory group (LDAP, OIDC) so its members join when they sign in.
groups.empty: Create a group to give permissions once to the group instead of to each person.
groups.name: The name you pick on the Permissions page (for example dev-team). It cannot change later.
groups.description: A short note on who is in the group. It shows in the list.

audit.intro: A record, kept on every node, of who did what, when and from where (IP). Requests that change something — sign-ins, creating and deleting VMs, changing settings — plus console opens and file-restore downloads are kept; requests that only read are not. Open a row to see all of it.
audit.empty: Widen the time range, or clear the user and action filters.

tasks.intro: Work that takes time, such as starting, moving or backing up VMs. See what is running, what finished, and why something failed.
tasks.empty: When you start, move or back up a VM, its progress and result collect here.

folders.intro: Group VMs, networks and storage into folders. Permissions given on a folder with 'Apply inside' pass down to what is inside, and VM folders can have quotas that cap the resources they use. Drag and drop to move things.
folders.empty: This folder is empty. Drag rows here or use Move to folder to put things in.
folders.name: The folder name (for example prod, team-a). Up to 64 characters, without '/'.
folders.folder: The folder the new item goes in. It gets the folder permissions given with 'Apply inside' and, for VM folders, counts toward the quota.
folders.destination: Where to move them. Moved items follow the permissions given on the new folder with 'Apply inside' and, for VM folders, its quota.
